description: ECHO PROOF is a two-person team participating in The Earth Information Jukebox challenge. We’re interested in Earth observation, data analysis, accessible data visualization, and translating scientific information into clear multisensory experiences. We’re working together during this hackathon and are not currently seeking additional team members.
summary:
ECHO PROOF is a browser-based deterministic sonification experience that translates spatial information in NASA Earth visualizations into sound. For its primary demonstration, it compares two NASA SVS 5675 frames showing the evolution of the Krasheninnikov lava field between June 18 and June 30, 2026.

Each image is divided into a fixed 6×4 grid. ECHO PROOF measures visual brightness density in every cell and maps that value deterministically to sound frequency and stereo position. Matched A/B playback lets users hear the same spatial region before and after the observed change, while the Translation Receipt exposes the mapping so the process remains inspectable and reproducible.

The same mapping principle is also transferred to NASA Black Marble Night Lights imagery from 2012 and 2023, demonstrating that the method can be reused across different Earth-observation stories.

ECHO PROOF does not classify lava or infer physical meaning from brightness; NASA provides the scientific interpretation of the source visualizations.
details:
ECHO PROOF is a browser-based interactive sonification application created for NASA Space Apps 2026 — The Earth Information Jukebox. It explores a focused question: can spatial change in a NASA Earth-observation visualization be translated into sound using a transparent and reproducible rule?

The PRIMARY experience uses NASA Scientific Visualization Studio SVS 5675 and compares two Krasheninnikov visualization frames labelled June 18 and June 30, 2026. Each frozen image uses the same fixed 6×4 grid. For every cell, ECHO PROOF measures display brightness density using the disclosed EP-MAP-1.0 rule: pixel luma is calculated from RGB values, pixels at or above a fixed threshold are counted, and the resulting bright-pixel fraction is mapped deterministically to tone frequency. Horizontal grid position determines stereo pan.

The same mapping configuration is used for both dates. “Hear the Change — Matched A/B” plays each June 18 cell immediately followed by the corresponding June 30 cell, making local before/after differences easier to hear without separately normalizing or tuning the two observations.

A secondary METHOD TRANSFER applies the same deterministic mapping principle to NASA Black Marble Night Lights annual visualizations for 2012 and 2023. This tests whether the approach can be reused on a different Earth-observation story without turning Night Lights into a second primary project. The Night Lights transfer uses the same disclosed brightness-density-to-frequency mapping family and was retained as secondary evidence after testing.

A central feature is the Translation Receipt. It exposes the mapping rule and per-cell values used to generate the audio, including brightness-density measurements, frequencies, stereo positions and before/after differences. The receipt is derived from the same runtime calculations that drive the sound, so users can inspect how the sonification was produced rather than treating it as a black box.

ECHO PROOF was built as a lightweight client-only web application using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, browser Canvas image processing and the Web Audio API. It has no backend, database, login, runtime AI model, runtime API calls, analytics, telemetry or user-data collection. The live application is hosted with GitHub Pages.

Source code, documentation, provenance records, licensing information, AI-use disclosure and release-integrity evidence are available in the public repository:

https://github.com/DaniKarmy/ECHO-PROOF

ECHO PROOF was developed through substantive human–AI collaboration. The human project lead contributed core project ideas and direction, including the decision to keep Krasheninnikov as the PRIMARY candidate until it received a proper evidence-based GO/NO-GO assessment rather than abandoning it prematurely. The human contribution also included retaining and validating Matched A/B as the principal “Hear the Change” presentation, proposing NASA Night Lights as a second Earth-observation perspective through which the same deterministic method could be tested, defining the final PRIMARY versus METHOD TRANSFER structure, reviewing scientific claim boundaries, performing decisive perceptual and runtime testing, shaping the application presentation and user experience, challenging results and proposed directions when they did not withstand review, and retaining final authority over release and submission.

The second team member contributed an independent second-user runtime and usability check of the public ECHO PROOF application before submission. He verified that the application loaded correctly, that the audio played normally, that the experience was understandable, and reported no observed errors or unclear elements.

ChatGPT assisted with research and rule verification, technical design, deterministic mapping development, code generation and debugging, test and verification support, security and release review, source and provenance checks, and documentation drafting. Project decisions and material outputs were not accepted automatically: approaches were repeatedly tested, challenged, revised, rejected or reinstated when evidence and human evaluation required it. The final application itself does not use an AI or LLM at runtime; its sonification is deterministic JavaScript and Web Audio logic.

Scientific interpretation is deliberately separated from the sonification algorithm. NASA identifies the evolving bright field in the Krasheninnikov visualization as lava; ECHO PROOF does not detect or classify lava and does not treat visual brightness as a lava probability, temperature, physical backscatter or other geological measurement. For Night Lights, the application likewise does not infer population, economic activity, urban growth, physical radiance or the cause of lighting changes from image brightness.

The intended impact is to demonstrate an additional, inspectable way to experience spatial change in Earth-observation imagery while preserving reproducibility, source provenance and clear scientific boundaries. ECHO PROOF does not claim to invent sonification itself. Its creative contribution is the specific combination of matched spatial before/after listening, one fixed deterministic mapping applied across observations, explicit scientific claim boundaries, and an auditable Translation Receipt that connects what the user sees to what the user hears.
